RouterOS runs a Linux kernel (5.6.3) but **everything above the kernel is MikroTik's proprietary `no
- No apt, pkg, opkg — no package manager (packages are `.npk` files installed via upload + reboot)
- No `docker`, `podman` — RouterOS has its own `/container` subsystem (7.x+)
- REST API at `/rest/` (HTTP, port 80 by default) — the primary programmatic interface
- RouterOS scripting language (`.rsc` files) — its own syntax, not bash. See [Scripting reference](.
- Do NOT try `ssh admin@host 'ls /'` — it opens RouterOS CLI, not a shell
- Do NOT suggest `mount`, `fdisk`, `mkfs` — use `/disk` commands instead
- Do NOT look for config files at `/etc/` — configuration is in the RouterOS database
- Do NOT assume `ping` works the same — it's `/tool/ping` or `/ping` in CLI
- Do NOT suggest installing packages via `apt` or `opkg` — upload `.npk` via SCP then `/system/packa
RouterOS REST API at `http://HOST:PORT/rest/`. HTTP verbs map non-standardly:
- `PUT` creates (NOT updates) — opposite of many REST APIs
- Empty password auth: `admin:` (colon required, nothing after)
- WebFig root (`GET /`) returns HTTP 200 without auth — use as health check
- REST API (`/rest/`) requires auth (HTTP 401 without it)

content.user_title: Manage RouterOS v7 With AI Agents
content.value_statement: RouterOS differs from standard Linux, so generic shell advice often fails. This skill gives Claude, Codex, and Claude Code RouterOS-specific CLI, REST API, and automation guidance.
actual_capabilities: Explains RouterOS CLI syntax and key differences from GNU/Linux systems.
Maps RouterOS REST verbs to CLI actions and common endpoint patterns.
Covers RouterOS v7 packages, licensing, users, SSH keys, networking, firewall rules, and device-mode behavior.
Documents async REST commands, blocking endpoints, timeout handling, and post-boot race conditions.
Provides examples for curl, TypeScript fetch, RouterOS scripts, and CHR automation workflows.
limitations: Covers RouterOS 7.x only; RouterOS v6 behavior may differ.
Reference files are not executable and do not connect to routers by themselves.
Some endpoint behavior is marked as CHR-specific or derived from documentation.
Live router validation requires separate authorized access and tooling.

use_cases.title: Plan RouterOS REST Changes
use_cases.description: Prepare safe REST API changes for firewall, users, packages, DNS, routes, and interfaces.

use_cases.title: Automate CHR Provisioning
use_cases.description: Build CHR setup flows that handle package enablement, reboot behavior, device-mode updates, and readiness polling.

use_cases.title: Translate Linux Assumptions
use_cases.description: Convert generic Linux commands into RouterOS CLI or REST workflows before generating operational instructions.

prompt_templates.title: Explain RouterOS Basics
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner orientation before changing a MikroTik router.
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain how RouterOS v7 differs from GNU/Linux for CLI, files, packages, and service management. Keep the answer practical for an AI agent.

prompt_templates.title: Plan A REST Task
prompt_templates.prompt: I need to change RouterOS v7 settings through REST. Identify the correct endpoint, HTTP verb, request shape, verification step, and any RouterOS gotchas.

prompt_templates.title: Review Firewall Changes
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this planned RouterOS firewall change for ordering, rule placement, verification, and lockout risk. Explain what should be checked before applying it.

prompt_templates.title: Design CHR Automation
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a CHR automation flow for RouterOS v7 that handles boot readiness, user setup, SSH keys, package changes, blocking REST commands, and post-change validation.

output_examples.input: How should I add an input firewall allow rule without breaking rule order?
output_examples.output: The skill explains that new firewall rules append by default. It recommends finding the existing drop rule, inserting before it, and verifying final order.

output_examples.input: Why does a RouterOS device-mode REST update appear to hang?
output_examples.output: It identifies the endpoint as blocking until power-cycle confirmation or timeout. It suggests a deadline, recovery handling, and post-boot verification.

output_examples.input: Can I use apt or normal Linux commands on RouterOS?
output_examples.output: It states that RouterOS has no Unix shell or Linux package manager. It directs the user to RouterOS CLI paths and package workflows.

best_practices: Confirm RouterOS version, hardware type, and lab versus production context before applying examples.
Replace placeholder hosts and local CHR addresses with authorized router targets only.
Back up configuration and verify router state after any REST or CLI change.
anti_patterns: Treating RouterOS SSH as a Linux shell with commands such as ls, apt, or systemctl.
Adding firewall rules without controlling placement or verifying evaluation order.
Running blocking REST commands without timeouts, polling, or recovery steps.

faq.question: Does this skill execute RouterOS commands?
faq.answer: No. It is reference material for AI agents and does not execute commands or make network requests by itself.

faq.question: Which RouterOS versions does it cover?
faq.answer: It targets RouterOS 7.x. RouterOS 6 behavior is outside scope and may be inaccurate.

faq.question: Can it help with the RouterOS REST API?
faq.answer: Yes. It documents verb mapping, common endpoints, authentication patterns, async commands, and response gotchas.

faq.question: Does it include firewall guidance?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers filter, NAT, mangle, rule ordering, placement, and verification patterns.

faq.question: Can it manage MikroTik licenses or credentials directly?
faq.answer: No. It only describes endpoint behavior and safe handling patterns. Users must provide authorized tooling and credentials.

faq.question: Is it useful for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code?
faq.answer: Yes. It provides domain context that helps those assistants avoid Linux assumptions when working on RouterOS tasks.
